items.title: Touch-screen OLED MacBook Pro expected in October or November
items.content_html:
Apple's long-expected MacBook Pro revision with the range's first OLED display and first touch-enabled screen was originally expected in the next few months, but is now likely to launch in the next few weeks.

While iPhone Duo pre-orders have not even started yet, and attention has turned to Apple's home products expected on October 13, the MacBook Pro redesign is also near. There is still a chance that it will slip to early 2027, but most recent leaks point to an October or November 2026 release.

The key change is to be the screen used for both the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 16-inch MacBook Pro. It's expected to be Apple's first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro, even though the company has previously decried the idea.

However, touchscreen displays have now been in Windows laptops for years. Then, too, Apple is looking to add compelling reasons for existing users to upgrade.

Potentially another such reason will be the introduction of an OLED display. OLED produces richer blacks and a higher quality image while using less battery power.

But Apple made OLED the distinction between the 13-inch iPad Air and 13-inch iPad Pro back in 2024, and it doesn't appear to have driven upgrades as much as expected.

items.title: Do not open links to an early iPhone Duo pre-order page
items.content_html:
Scammers have launched what is claimed to be a pre-order site for the iPhone Duo, but if you are on an older iOS, simply going to the page installs malware.

Genuine iPhone Duo pre-orders start on October 16, 2026, and Apple is now promoting that you can "get ready" from October 12. If you're interested, follow the links on AppleInsider, or go straight to apple.com.

Not to overplay this, if you already have iOS 26 or later, or if you have the latest update to iOS 18, you should be safe. This latest attack appears to use the DarkSword malware, and Apple patched iOS to protect against this in April 2026.

Even so, simply do not go to any "pre-order" site that is sent to you over email, or Messages. Don't even go out of curiosity, because according to Malwarebytes, just opening the page is enough.

The site in question, which of course no one will link to, is reportedly very well designed and looks like an Apple one. It also looks comparatively innocent, since it does not ask for money, it asks users to express interest in pre-ordering.

It even offers a $500 voucher and AppleCare+ coverage for filling out that form. If you've been around Apple long enough, this should alert you because the company would never give a quarter off the retail price of anything.

Then, too, while the iPhone Duo is not yet available, details of it such as the available colors, are well known. This particular scam site lists colors that do not even exist.

The scam requires users to be on the Safari browser, but it will also take steps to make sure they are. If you were foolish enough to go to the page in any other app, you'd get "Browser Restricted."

On the iPhone, you get that plus it automatically opens Safari for you. DarkSword then attempts to bypass iOS security.

If it succeeds, because the iPhone has not been updated to include Apple's security patch, then the malware goes to work. It sends device details, passwords from the keychain, the contents of Apple Notes, and multiple cryptocurrency wallets.

Then it accesses, or tries to access, call history, voicemails, email, calendar entries, and even location data.

Again, be sure to update your iPhone's iOS. Under Settings, General, Software Update, tap to install the latest iOS version available for your iPhone. There is also an option for Automatic Updates and you should turn that on, too.

Rather than clicking on any link sent to you, always open a browser window and go directly to the vendor's website. If the offer is real, it will be there too.

But also just be aware. It's no one's job to remember order dates and model colors or specifications. Yet if a deal seems to be too good to be true, such as $500 off an iPhone Duo, it is.

items.title: Latest Apple TV outage is persisting for some users
items.content_html:
Multiple Apple Services went down late afternoon on September 30, 2026, and Apple TV continues to be unavailable for an unknown number of users.

Initially the outage hit Apple Music, Apple Fitness+, the App Store and more as well as Apple TV. Compared to when it went down for the launch of "Pluribus," it was a quiet time for there to be problems, but Apple TV is reportedly still having issues.

AppleInsider testing shows it working internationally, and DownDetector says there are no longer any problems. However Apple's own system status page says that Apple TV has not yet been fully restored.

Listing the problem as beginning at 4:43 PM Eastern, Apple says it is ongoing and that "some users are affected."

At the same time, the status page notes that "Apple TV may be unavailable due to scheduled maintenance." That phrasing suggests that the maintenance is unrelated to the outage.

Apple doesn't usually take services offline for maintenance, however.

items.title: Meta Muse AI reportedly read Mac Messages without consent
items.content_html:
In a completely unsurprising turn of events, Meta's Muse AI is stealing Apple Messages, past and present, and uploading the contents to its cloud, even if explicitly told not to.

If you use Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, or WhatsApp, you've probably been inundated with prompts to try out Meta's next big questionable service: Muse. And it's not like Meta, the parent company of Facebook, has a great track record regarding privacy, safety, or ethics.

If you're not in the know, Muse is Meta's AI agent designed to help with tasks such as researching topics, preparing briefings, and shopping. According to Meta, it runs on a dedicated virtual computer and can use information from connected apps and data sources to tailor its responses.

Meta says that Muse has to obey permissions that users set up. It won't access any data you don't explicitly allow it to access.

Of course, Meta also hedges, a lot, right at the top of the "How Muse works..." page, saying:

"Your Muse can make mistakes or take unexpected actions," Meta says. No kidding.

I've never used Muse, and frankly, I never will. I'll get into why later.

But Jason Aten over at Inc has. What he's learned is, unfortunately, horrifying.

Aten installed Muse on both his iPhone and a Mac mini that he uses to test out various AI agents and tech. It took Meta a single day to begin "helpfully" pitching article ideas based on texts he'd sent to a podcast co-host.

When he asked Muse how it got the information, it said that it read banners from incoming texts. But that's not true, either.

After doing a little digging, Aten says Muse synced 187,000 lines from his Messages database, despite Full Disk Access being off.

A screenshot of a Threads post where Jason Aten shows Muse synced Messages without permission

I'd like you to read that a second time. Meta's similarly named Messenger app didn't get ingested.

Apple's Messages did.

Unless Aten is the most popular person on the face of the planet, I sincerely doubt he'd gotten 187,000 lines of text in roughly 24 hours. What happened is that, without permission, Muse went into the app and downloaded the information.

He had not given Muse permission to access Messages, and full disk access was not enabled. It just went ahead and uploaded those texts anyway.

Muse can take "unexpected actions" indeed.

Ignoring AI ingestion, Meta is not a company I would trust with any private information anyway. It seems that it's in a race to the bottom, primarily with itself.

It was just over a year ago that the company had asked Facebook users for permission to continuously upload their entire camera roll to its cloud. Meta said this was to "create ideas for posts" for its users, and it would analyze the images for time, location, and themes.

I take a lot of pictures of things that I don't want Meta accessing, and you do too. For me, it's nieces, nephews, medical bills, grievous leg wounds, funny vanity license plates, and probably thousands of embarrassing selfies I send my sister.

None of these are intended to be shared with a company that repeatedly steps on any available rake when it comes to privacy issues.

And just under a year ago, we learned that Meta Ray-Ban Display, Meta's take on smart glasses, has been used by many wearers to violate the privacy and safety of anyone around them. There's even an entire smart glasses subculture dedicated to disabling the lights that make it obvious when the wearers are filming.

I'm not entirely sure what Meta's end goal is, other than to figure out how to turn every single person into a perpetual data generation machine for its company.

And the punchline is, this whole Muse debacle is yet another trumpet blaring as we barrel full speed ahead into the oncoming AI privacy apocalypse. At what point is it too late to solve these problems?

If the agents are already blatantly ignoring the guardrails, are we already past the point of no return?

I think what sticks in my craw about this the most is the fact that Meta has ensured that you do not get the option to opt out. No matter who you are, Meta has found a way to harvest your data.

Prompts to download Muse in WhatsApp, Instagram, and an ad for Muse in the iOS App Store

You could never create a single account on a single Meta service, of which there are many, and you still aren't safe. If you're talking to someone who has installed Muse, Meta could, presumably, access, read, analyze, and upload that information to its services.

And this is the point where I need to step back and point out that this isn't just a Meta issue. I'm naming-and-shaming Meta here because we've got countless examples of Meta's tape-and-bubblegum safety guards failing.

But every company that is investing in AI wants carte blanche access to your information. It doesn't matter if it's Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, or even Apple.

Big tech companies want one thing, and it's disgusting.

I mean, hell, Apple Intelligence can already access things like Messages and Mail. The defining difference here is trust. Apple Intelligence, at present, attempts to process much of the request on-device.

That's a big reason why Apple Intelligence is relegated to more-powerful Apple chips.

In the event that something does need to be processed off-device, Apple says that only the relevant data is sent to Private Cloud Compute.

We're entering an era where privacy does not exist. At one point, the stock advice to people who were concerned about this very thing was "Well, if you don't like it, don't use it.

But that doesn't protect you anymore. Muse can get access to your information via people who do use it. Apple has made Apple Intelligence non-optional on compatible devices.

This is it, dear reader. You don't get to opt out anymore.

items.title: Oppo can't get accusations of Apple Watch trade secret theft dismissed
items.content_html:
A federal judge didn't buy Oppo's OpenAI-like arguments about IP theft by an engineer that allegedly took Apple Watch trade secrets to Oppo.

In August 2025, Apple accused ex-employee Chen Shi of sharing confidential Apple Watch details with Chinese rival Oppo. According to Courthouse News, he is accused of having done so in order to secure a job with what US District Judge Eumi Lee calls "a generous salary."

Now Judge Lee has ruled that the case can proceed. Specifically, she said that Apple's claims of breach of contract alone are sufficient that she would not dismiss the case.

In her six-page ruling, Judge Lee uses the word "plausibly" to describe Apple's allegations 14 times. In a similar move to OpenAI in its current case with Apple, Oppo argued that the information in question was not a trade secret.

Judge Lee ruled that Apple has made specific allegations concerning at least one trade secret.

Oppo's argument was also that Apple uses the term trade secret so broadly that Shi "cannot practice as an engineer in the health-sensing field without violating it."

Judge Lee disagreed, saying that the Intellectual Property Agreement (IPA) that Shi signed with Apple only precludes him from disclosing confidential company information.

As detailed in the ruling, Apple alleges that, "late at night just three days before leaving Apple, Dr Shi downloaded 63 documents," which he transferred to a USB drive. Prior to leaving, he also "set up and attended dozens of one-on-one meetings with Apple Watch technical team members to learn about their ongoing research."

Separately, it's been alleged that Shi told Apple he was leaving to care for family members, and not that he was joining Oppo. He's also accused of having searched online for ways to cover up his actions, such as searching for "can somebody see if I've opened a file on a shared drive."

Oppo is not a well-known name in the US. But, its smartwatches are a key rival to the Apple Watch in China.

Defendants Guangdong Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Ltd. and InnoPeak Technology, Inc. now have until October 21, 2026, to file a responsive pleading. That means filing specific defenses against Apple's allegations.

That's significant because up to now, Oppo has reportedly failed to cooperate with discovery. The court ordered Oppo to comply by October 31, 2025.

There was also a deadline for Shi to take part in a deposition, but he asked for it to be extended. Reportedly around this time he had been diagnosed with a condition that could worsen if he were in "a lengthy, high-stress, and adversarial proceeding."

It's not clear whether that deposition has been rescheduled. It does appear, though, that Oppo has continued to delay complying with the discovery order.

That delay is not part of the new ruling about Apple having plausible reason to sue. Separately, Apple claimed in March 2026 that it needed an emergency injunction to prevent Oppo deleting evidence.

Judge Lee is reportedly still considering this request. What's most likely to happen next, then, is that she will rule over that preliminary injunction.

Other than the October 21, 2026 deadline for responsive pleading, no further dates regarding the case have been published.

Judge Lee is also presiding over a separate iCloud case. In 2025, she ruled in favor of consumers pressing for a case to be heard against Apple.

items.title: Making millions of iPhone Duos is proving harder than Apple hoped
items.content_html:
Only Apple knows what it expected for yields, but manufacturers are claiming that the iPhone Duo is difficult to manufacture at scale, with its folding screen and hinge complicating production.

Assembly yields for the iPhone Duo remain low, while component delays have shortened the time available to refine production. Apple now faces a familiar foldable phone problem: producing millions of units that reliably work.

Foxconn's iPhone Duo assembly yield is just above 60%, according to supply chain sources speaking to Jiemian News. The first production batch is small, and the line still needs repeated adjustments.

One source estimated that yields could take six months to a year to mature under Apple's current standards. How this will affect shipping times remains to be seen, but we expect significant delays.

The sources said the low yield does not stem from a single unresolved technical problem. Equipment, processes, and production settings need refinement as the line moves toward larger volumes.

Samsung Display's OLED panels and hinge components made by other manufacturers have also faced insufficient yields and delayed deliveries. Each upstream delay leaves less time for Foxconn to improve assembly yields.

And, as expected, the very thing that makes the iPhone Duo a duo is responsible for many delays: the hinge.

The hinge contains more than 100 parts working together under tight tolerances. Even relatively small differences can wildly affect how the device functions.

Apple reportedly reconsidered using liquid metal in some hinge parts before mass production, but ultimately decided on a different solution. If it were to revise the process, it would require new prototypes and functional samples, verification, and supplier adjustments.

Historically, Apple has considered manufacturing yields an assembler issue. It's not clear what Apple was expecting for a percentage of devices off the line passing quality inspections.

Apple could, theoretically, relax its standards to allow for more saleable units, but that seems improbable. The supplier could also push its production line harder, though it would likely lead to more units completed, but at a higher percentage of defective units.

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo as part of its "Surprise and Shine" Apple Event on September 12; it starts at an eye-watering $1,999, before taxes. Apple set October 16 for preorders and October 23 for release, which was notably longer after the initial announcement than even the iPhone X.

items.title: Refreshed HomePod mini, Apple TV and new HomeHub coming on October 13
items.content_html:
A new report claims that Apple is planning October 13 for the unveiling of a trio of home products, including the much-awaited HomeHub or HomePod.

It's already been leaked that the HomePod mini refresh will be confined to new colors, and the updated Apple TV 4K will keep its existing chassis design. According to Bloomberg, these two are set to be released alongside the brand-new home hub.

As previously reported, that HomePod with a screen has been waiting only for the updated Siri AI to be released. All three of these devices were reportedly first scheduled to launch as long ago as 2024.

No details of pricing or really of any configuration is known for the home hub, although there have been code leaks that describe how its screen will work. The device is also believed to check for nearby iPhones, and then display relevant data for that user.

Intended to be used by multiple people, this device is expected to act as a central control unit of your Apple Home. It's previously been reported to launch in 2024, 2025, and most recently in late 2026.

The colors of the refreshed HomePod mini lineup colors are expected to be black, white, blue, pink, and green. It's also expected that four such HomePod minis could be paired to an Apple TV 4K, too.

The new Apple TV 4K is coming soon

Then the new Apple TV 4K is presumed to bring Siri AI to the TV set for the first time, and it's rumored to feature both an A20 Pro processor and a doubling of RAM to 8GB. Those are needed for Siri AI but will also benefit gamers.

The existing larger HomePod is said to be getting a refresh as well, but not alongside this launch. Apple is also planning home security devices, which are currently expected to launch in 2027.

Apple is not expected to release any other brand-new devices, but according to the new report, it is working with other companies. Apple is said to be revising its HomeKit software to better support third-party devices.

items.title: iPhone Duo expected to sell 6M units by end of 2026
items.content_html:
Apple will sell approximately 6 million units of the iPhone Duo in 2026, according to analysts' forecast, which may be more promising than it first appears.

The iPhone Duo has yet to go on sale, but that hasn't stopped analysts from declaring what they believe the sales will be for the foldable model. In the case of one forecast from Counterpoint Research, that figure may seem to be a disappointment at first glance.

Apple could sell around 6 million units in 2026, Counterpoint told Bloomberg. Analyst Ivan Lam says that the final figure will depend on how well Apple ramps up production for the new model.

The production woes of the iPhone Duo were prominent in pre-launch rumors, but they have persisted. In a Tuesday report, Foxconn's assembly yield is allegedly just above 60%, with it unlikely to reach Apple's high standards for six months to a year.

It's fair to say that 6 million units isn't a massive amount on the Apple manufacturing scale. Far from it.

When it comes to the main iPhone lineup, Apple is predicted to be making approximately 80 million iPhones in total between Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. That six-month period incorporates the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max as well as the iPhone Duo, with the non-foldable models making up the lion's share.

The 6 million figure is for sales of the iPhone Duo in the last months of 2026, a shorter timeframe from the six-month overall production forecast.

While only a small segment of Apple's overall product mix, it's still a lot of units. To Counterpoint, 6 million units is closer to what you'd expect a production run of a foldable smartphone would have, rather than for an iPhone.

Even at this lower level, the iPhone Duo is expected to help increase interest and sales in foldable devices, including for its rivals. There's also the benefit of extra interest in Apple's mainstream iPhone lineup too just from the existence of the foldable model.

Considering the production line immaturity and the scale of sales forecasts relative to the rest of the folding smartphone market, the iPhone Duo doesn't seem to have a particularly bad future ahead of it. Production issues can usually be fixed and improved upon with time.

Think of it as the typical teething issues of a first-gen Apple product. The initial launch is to raise awareness and to shake out the problems, before coming in with an improved second version in the future.

items.title: Apple Invites update leans on iOS 27's new features
items.content_html:
An update for Apple Invites is making it better for users to create invitations and to relive their events in high resolution, with the iPhone app tapping into some of the features of iOS 27.

The introduction of a new operating system version usually is accompanied by updates to Apple's apps to best take advantage of any new features it includes. With iOS 27 now out on iPhones, Apple Invites has undergone the same treatment.

The update to version 1.12.0 released on September 30 includes three main feature changes, alongside the usual bug fixes and performance improvements.

The first is that Shared Albums now support full-resolution sharing, so party participants can share images from the event with each other without the images being made smaller. This applies both to users with Apple devices and those who do not but have been invited to the party.

Image Playgrounds was previously used to generate backgrounds, but that too has been updated. This includes adopting the new photorealistic options, accessible in the normal version of Image Playgrounds too.

Lastly, Apple has made it easier to verify guests' email addresses. While previously they had to enter a code, the verification emails now include a link that can be tapped to do the same thing.

Previous updates include a June change enabling emoji replies and a confetti animation.

Apple Invites is free, weighs in at 113MB, and requires iOS 26.0 or later.

items.title: India finally gets Apple Pay after more than nine years of negotiations
items.content_html:
Apple has launched Apple Pay in India for the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, with Mac support to follow. It follows years of negotiating the country's complex financial legislation.

Apple Pay was first unveiled for the US back in 2014, and since then has been steadily rolling out around the world. Yet despite Eddy Cue expressly saying in 2017 that Apple was trying to bring it to India, it has taken until now to happen.

"India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy," said Jennifer Bailey, Apple's vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet in a statement, "and we're so excited to bring Apple Pay to users in India today."

Apple Pay is initially available only via Visa and Mastercard credit cards issued by India's Axis Bank. Apple says that payments "will be accepted by millions of merchants across India," including merchant networks such as BillDesk, Cashfree, and Juspay.

"We are at a significant inflection point in payments, where technology, security and changing customer expectations are reshaping how people transact," said Amitabh Chaudhry, MD & CEO, Axis Bank. "At Axis Bank, our aspiration is to remain at the forefront of this transformation by building payment experiences that are progressive, trusted and deeply relevant to our customers."

Apple has yet to give a date for when Apple Pay will be supported on Macs in India. It has said, though, that the feature is "coming soon."

One of the reasons for the delay getting Apple Pay into India is that from June 2022, the country added extra financial laws. There was also complexity over biometric identification, as India required firms to use its Aadhaar ID system instead of Face ID.

These laws also covered online recurring payments, such as subscriptions. Specifically, they required banks to notify users 24 hours in advance of any recurring transaction, and allow them to cancel it.

That by itself won't have stopped Apple Pay, but the change was sufficient that Apple ceased accepting any debit or credit cards.

Users had to instead pay via India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI). That didn't change even when Apple opened its first Apple Stores in India back in 2023.

Starting in January 2026, it was rumored that Apple was close to getting Apple Pay in India. Then by July 2026, there were reports that Apple was again accepting card payments, and that it was part of complying with Indian regulations to help it launch Apple Pay.

items.title: Code hints continue to reveal features of Apple's upcoming Home Hub
items.content_html:
The long-rumored Home Hub tablet device seems to contain an assortment of features from across Apple's ecosystem, and a code sleuth has found a connection between it and iPhone Duo.

Apple's Home Hub is expected to be revealed on October 13 as a tablet device that is carried around the home. Rumors suggest it will display content based on who is nearby or interacting with the device, but very little has been shared otherwise.

Code sleuth and leaker pdfu shared that setting up the Home Hub will include creating a Photo Face. The Photo Face is one that will also be used in the new iPhone Duo StandBy feature.

The Photo Face makes sense for the Home Hub, as it will display something when not in use. The code doesn't provide a name beyond a placeholder of "Apple device."

Setting up Apple's upcoming Home device includes a new step: creating a Photo Face.

It's the same Photo Face coming to StandBy on iPhone Duo. That might explain why Apple hasn't officially made StandBy available in the simulator.

Photo Face requires iCloud Photos. During setup, pic.twitter.com/Zh3cvAcjPx

Users will be able to select from shuffling photos, showing Memory slideshows, or pulling content from shared albums. Then users will get the chance to select photos manually or pick from specific collections or simply use featured photos chosen by the device.

The screenshots are tall and skinny, suggesting a modal shown over content, so there is nothing to derive from the images themselves. However, the previewed images are square, which fits in with previous rumors that Apple's Home Hub tablet could have a square display.

The leaker shared on Monday that code hinted at Apple offering more StandBy faces and configurations, but they were hidden in the device simulator. Based on the latest Photo Face discovery, it seems Apple could be keeping some features hidden until the Home Hub is revealed.

New OS updates mean more code to delve through, and pdfu has shared several discoveries, including how Tap to Pay on iPhone looks on iPhone Duo. It can be done on either display.

iPhone Duo supports Tap to Pay on both displays, featuring an adaptive interface. pic.twitter.com/EmtQWCXe8c

They've also discovered that the Snoopy screen saver on Apple TV will gain audio at some point, though the files aren't available to examine just yet.

These discoveries are likely tied to Apple not always being perfect in its cleanup of pre-release files in beta software. pdfu has been reliable and accurate in finding and sharing discoveries, like finding that Touch ID would be used in the iPhone Duo.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras are Apple's best yet, but only when you squint
items.content_html:
I'm in the bag for iPhone Duo, but I wanted to test out an iPhone 18 Pro Max camera system before going all in on Apple's foldable. Here's what I learned as I prepare for a potential camera downgrade.

I would love nothing more than to travel to some remote part of the planet and detail exactly how iPhone 18 Pro Max performs while showing off incredible one-of-a-kind photos. That isn't what I'm here to do today.

My simple goal is to explain exactly what I have observed about Apple's latest camera system, coming from the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and what buying an iPhone Duo might mean losing out on.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max showcases exactly what makes Apple's smartphone camera such a well-balanced and all-around great camera system. It's yet another pinnacle in years of slight improvements.

Photos captured on both iPhones are in the Bright Photographic Style at about -40 tone and +38 color.

I've got my trusty Sony a7II from 2014 that continues to produce amazing results straight from the sensor, RAW or not. I always shoot full manual with that camera and have no interest in the automatic settings.

So, it might be odd to say that I behave exactly the opposite on iPhone. For years, I downloaded the pro-level camera apps, tinkered with my workflow, edited every image to death — it was a tad exhausting at times.

There had to be a better way.

I wanted more control and a more unique look to my photos than what capturing straight from the iPhone camera could give me. Editing and filters often felt overprocessed and unrealistic.

I wanted to capture photos quickly and easily without fiddling with all those little digital dials and settings. I also wanted a workflow that was non-destructive and easily changed later.

Photographic Styles bring non-destructive customization to every photo

Apple gave me exactly what I wanted with Photographic Styles. The fully-reversible non-destructive shooting modes that could be preset and forget transformed how I approached mobile photography.

My big camera still sits at full manual and offers me control when I want it. My iPhone, on the other hand, is basically full auto with custom Photographic Styles.

I stopped shooting Apple ProRAW except in circumstances where I specifically knew I'd like more editing control. Photographic Styles are just that good.

The issue has never been about a lack of control, as that could be solved with third-party apps, it's the lack of physical controls. Apple tried to solve this with the poorly-executed Camera Control, which ends up being too fiddly as anything more than a shutter button.

Camera Control didn't get any of the new pro controls on iPhone 18 Pro Max

Apple is already showing signs of being done with Camera Control — the new pro camera tools aren't even part of it. I expect it'll be gone in a generation or two.

I'd love to see Apple make a physical camera with knobs and dials for each minute setting, but that isn't going to happen. The iPhone is inherently a point-and-shoot experience, and I'm okay with that.

I'll never complain about having more options for precise control, but they're going to be used as an exception to the norm. Nearly every photo captured will be done with the press of a shutter and nothing else.

That's the beauty of Photographic Styles. Take the photos you want now at whatever preset you've chosen and change them later as needed.

I like a camera that I can point and click the shutter, even my Sony a7II can function that way thanks to a back-button focus I have set up. I adjust the dials when needed, but most of the time I can set them and just capture photos until conditions change.

iPhone and Photographic Styles lets me do the same, if not even more efficiently. iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, is a step in the opposite direction in some cases.

Apple's approach to variable aperture is likely one of necessity. The iPhone 18 Pro Max Main Fusion camera is f/1.48 fully open.

Variable aperture only gets you so much control on a sensor that small

The problem is, until now, all iPhones shot photos fully open. There wasn't a physical aperture to close and let in less light.

Previous recent models shot at around f/1.78, which produced a soft bokeh when close enough to the subject. The subject was still sharp while plenty of light was gathered — it was the perfect set point for something that couldn't be changed.

Then arrives the f/1.48 sensor. It's "better" in that it can let in more light, meaning faster shutter speeds and better ISO (less noise).

The problem is you definitely do not want to shoot at that level all the time. With this sensor, f/1.48 is at the edge of beginning to lose sharpness in the subject.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max will default to f/1.8 for most shots and automatically switch to f/1.48 in low-light settings. The f/2.8 setting is a bit sharper even if it lets in less light, while f/4.0 is the max and loses sharpness again.

You'll use f/4.0 in the brightest of settings to ensure all faces are in focus in a cluster of people, for example. It's also great in dimmer or complex lighting environments where the aperture creates a "star" wherever pinpoints of light are visible.

The star looks best at f/2.8 in my opinion, but some may not like them at all, as they are technically a flaw in the photo being captured. The star results from how bright light is shown on the sensor through the aperture blades.

iPhone 18 Pro Max has a sun star effect when the aperture is anything other than full open

I appreciate this level of control in my iPhone camera. That said, it does feel a bit fiddly.

I expect the friction and fiddly nature of variable aperture on iPhone will ultimately result in me relying on the automatic setting. I'm enthusiastic about it now in my testing, but I'm certain I'd only rarely choose to change that toggle.

After variable aperture, the first thing you'll notice in a one-to-one comparison is how Photographic Styles has changed. It appears Apple has tweaked the pipeline and application values that result in slightly different, more refined looks versus the previous version.

Variable aperture isn't a reason to jump ship from iPhone 17 Pro Max

Upon further investigation, there is also a difference in how the iPhone deals with white balance. There is a pro tool for choosing white balance compensation on iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it's set to auto by default.

Whatever has changed with white balance behavior is noticeable in some light. It sometimes feels like an overcorrection, which is why you might want to use the manual control.

The available pro tools are great to have in the Apple Camera app. Shutter speed is something I love being able to control, as that is how you can get light trails in some situations.

Third-party apps can control these aspects of the iPhone camera, so that's not exactly new. It's a little weird that Apple doesn't include the pro camera controls in iPhone Duo or other non-pro iPhones.

I think third-party apps will be the better place to control these aspects of iPhone photography. The only reason you might use the Camera app to control these aspects is if you still want access to Apple's full camera pipeline.

Pro camera controls are exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro models

Minus the pro camera controls I mentioned, all of this is coming to iPhone Duo. The new Photographic Styles, updated processing, and white balance differences will be present in Apple's foldable.

In my previous camera spec breakdown, I found that the two most notable differences between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo will be the existence of an optical telephoto camera and variable aperture.

Nearly every other aspect is identical, which means iPhone Duo users shouldn't be worried about having a "worse" camera experience. Funny enough, for me at least, there may not be that much difference.

Like everyone else, I won't have an iPhone Duo to test until October 23, so that aspect will have to wait for another day. For now, I can only address what I've learned about iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Specs suggest iPhone Duo will have great cameras

I wish I had more time with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I'm perfectly aware of my limited time, so take what I have to say here with that in mind.

From what I can tell without holding an iPhone Duo in hand, I believe my previous conclusion stands true: optical telephoto and variable aperture are all I'll miss on iPhone Duo.

What I gain will be a foldable with new camera abilities like Smart Take and Duo FaceTime. Whether or not that's an equivalent exchange will be determined at a later date.

Like with Apple Watch Ultra, I believe a lot of iPhone "Pro" features fall into aspirational purchase territory. It's not that I don't consider myself a "professional" photographer, or find iPhone's pro controls too unwieldy, just that they're unnecessary for most applications.

The variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro Max doesn't have enough range to capture photos like the fountain example above. The water looks like that on the Sony a7II because I could set the aperture to f/22 and allow very little light in during a longer exposure.

When I use my Sony a7II camera, I'm using it the same way a professional might by taking control of every aspect of each photo using the device's physical controls. The interface and physicality of that camera leans into it being used as a professional tool.

When I shoot photos with my iPhone, I'm just pressing the shutter and letting the device do the rest. Photographic Styles give me enough control to ensure every photo I capture is uniquely mine, so I don't feel the need to dive deeper into the settings.

Too much control can lead to you missing the shot

Photographic Styles 3 with texture and grain options is available on iPhone Duo. Apple is not including pro controls, so no manual white balance, shutter speed, or access to a histogram will be available.

Here's the thing, I don't know that I'll even notice or care. If I need control over those things, I can access them in third-party apps.

When I was testing iPhone 18 Pro Max as a camera, I noticed how much time I spent in menus selecting each little tool set point. I would take a couple of shots, then back to those menus.

iPhones make great cameras because they're the one you have on you

The more photos I shot, the less time I spent adjusting anything manually. It was just too time-consuming to adjust aperture manually for each shot or worry about shutter speed.

As I've always inevitably learned with the iPhone, it is better to just point and shoot. If I want to have more control for a specific shot, there are third-party apps or Apple's controls available.

Thanks to that mentality, it means my photo-shooting experience will be very similar on iPhone Duo. Even the variable aperture fades to the background since most photos are taken at f/1.8.

iPhone Duo will capture all photos at f/1.78.

An iPhone couldn't take this photo

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple's best camera system yet. It has the most options for manual control, includes an interesting variable aperture, and has the best image pipeline so far.

That variable aperture is interesting, and in a generation or two, it'll be so good it'll be hard to miss. Today, the gains provided by it are minimal, and only a good eye will spot the difference in most shots.

If you're anything like me, there won't be much to miss when choosing the iPhone Duo. It is still an iPhone camera system, and a powerful one at that with A20 Pro and Photographic Styles 3.

I have no doubt that future Apple foldables will have pro-level camera systems. Today, iPhone Duo doesn't, which makes it a primary purchase decision between the two devices.

This write up was for the photography nerds like me. Most iPhone users won't be able to spot the difference between shots on an iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro without being told what to look for.

That Charmander figure is softer and less defined here thanks to the iPhone's f/1.48 wide open aperture.

It's a big leap in performance and function, don't get me wrong. However, even the big leaps only show through so much on an already amazing camera system.

For those just wondering how it compares with previous iPhone cameras, think of it this way: your iPhone is already the best camera you own. The only differences an upgrade will bring is better experiences at the fringes.

You'll always capture pristine and beautiful photos in broad daylight. Dim and night photos will prove a challenge to even the best smartphone cameras, but Apple's latest systems perform marginally better over previous ones.

iPhone 18 Pro Max gives photographers more control than ever

iPhone 18 Pro Max is about control. However, I'm increasingly wondering how much control we actually need when the cameras are this good.

I'm glad the options are there, first or third-party, but it just goes to show how good the iPhone has become as a camera that the controls are almost unnecessary. I'm aware that these thoughts might reflect my own journey as a photographer more than what is true of Apple's offering, so your miles may vary.

The thing is, I don't feel this way about my dedicated camera. It's more akin to using a record player — deliberate and thoughtful.

When I pull out my Sony camera, I'm setting out on a photographic journey to accomplish a shot I'm envisioning using the controls in my hands. When I pull out my iPhone, I'm looking to capture a moment or a memory in an instant.

I matched the Sony's settings with the result from the iPhone, which produced a dimmer shot. That's mostly due to the exposure stacking iPhone performs with every shot.

Each of these devices serves different purposes and reaches different goals. When photographing people, the big camera draws attention, for better or for worse, and changes the environment you're photographing by the nature of the device.

The iPhone can show up and not draw anyone's eye, though I'm sure that'll be an issue for the iPhone Duo for a time. In any case, there's something more fleeting and unserious about capturing an iPhone photo.

I'm over 2.3k words into this, so I'll keep this bit short. I spent a day at a pumpkin patch with my friends recently and had three cameras on my person — iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Sony a7II.

A still frame of the spatial video captured on iPhone 18 Pro Max

I took about 80 keepable photos and some video during the day, with about 39 on my Sony a7II. The sun was too bright and over-exposing everything, so it was a challenging shooting day for full-manual controls.

Nearly every other photo was taken on the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and zero with the telephoto camera. I wanted to reserve the iPhone 18 Pro Max, deliberately, for situations I thought called for that specific device.

None arose, though I did capture a spatial video in the corn maze with it.

There are a few photos I really like from the iPhone, as they captured casual situations more easily. A few exemplified the speed at which I could get a photo when using an iPhone versus a larger camera.

I snuck a few photos with the iPhone 17 Pro Max while recording video with the iPhone 18 Pro Max

Nearly all of my favorite shots came from the Sony a7II. Not just because it is a superior full-frame camera with a powerful lens, but because they felt more deliberate.

I took the time to compensate for lighting whether we were in the sun or shade, using the easy-to-use controls on the camera. Adjusting these things on the fly was intuitive and simple compared to the digital touch interface of an iPhone.

Some shots were a bit out of focus or had motion blurring where the iPhone wouldn't have allowed it. However, there's something I can't quite put my finger on that separates the "quality" of the two images.

Of course, no smartphone can truly compete with a full-frame camera. There is a reason professionals still buy them over simply shooting with an iPhone for everything.

iPhone 18 Pro Max is incredible in spite of its small camera sensors

That's the point I'm reaching for, though I'm not sure I'm conveying it well. Apple wants iPhone 18 Pro Max to reflect the performance and control of a high-end full-frame camera, but falls short due to a lack of dedicated physical controls and sensor size.

Physics will always win in this contest. There isn't space for good physical camera controls on iPhone, nor is there room for larger sensors.

My point is, pros will always choose the bigger camera when possible. However, the power of the iPhone is that it is always on your person, therefore winning as the best camera for that reason.

Though, because of the physical limitations of a smartphone, I think it makes more sense to lean into automatic settings and systems like Photographic Styles. It's great more control is available to those that need it, but very few people will.

iPhone accessories never quite recreate the dedicated camera experience

I wouldn't mind seeing more accessories for iPhone that bring pro-level physical controls to iPhone. Apple should build more APIs to allow that, but that's a conversation for another day.

To bring this thing to a close, I'll share this: iPhone 18 Pro Max is amazing, and in some ways, better even than the iPhone 17 Pro Max I still possess. However, iPhone cameras have gotten so good that simply getting the shot and worrying about the details later is the way to go in 99% of situations.

The iPhone Duo will get Photographic Styles 3 with texture and grain control, so I'll dive more into that when I'm testing the foldable. I can already tell that I'll love grain when it is warranted, but it can be too aggressive at times.

Smart Take and Kid Cue are features exclusive to iPhone Duo

I'm glad I took the time to test out the iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras myself. I can now say quite confidently that even as good as the upgrades are, they're ones I can and will live without.

Next up, iPhone Duo as a camera. If my assumptions are right, the only thing I will truly miss is the optical telephoto 4x camera and the lack of spatial video capture support.

I have zero doubt iPhone Duo will capture photos just as good as iPhone 18 Pro Max in most day-to-day situations. I'll share those experiences later in October.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro's development graveyard exemplifies Apple's '1,000 no's to every yes'
items.content_html:
Pundits continue to hold up clear signs of restraint as failures while asking Apple to behave like Meta, OpenAI, Google, or anyone else but themselves, especially when discussing Apple Vision Pro.

If any of Apple's thousands of employees dare leave the company, or if one of hundreds of internal prototypes doesn't make it to production, you better believe punditry will be there to let us know.

The critical analysis almost always suffers from the same problem: asking Apple to chase the puck to where it is today, not where it is going.

Look, there are a dozen Steve Jobs-isms that I can throw in here that should tell you exactly how Apple operates. It is one of the most scrutinized companies on Earth, and yet, reporting in the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg can't help but ask Apple to change its behavior.

That Apple essence may confound analysts and pontificators, but one thing has held true in its long history: don't bet against it.

The focus of the week is on Meta's new "VR Glasses" that are neither VR nor glasses. Sure, they weigh 1/6 less and cost 1/3 the price, but they're also half the spec.

Apple Vision Pro has a weight problem, absolutely, but let us not pretend that Apple is actually okay with sacrificing fidelity and scope for that simple metric. Even this report shows the lengths of the research and prototyping Apple went through to try and get a smaller device sooner, but chose to say "no."

But of course, in light of Meta's "yes" with Meta VR Glasses, Apple's no's need to be seen as a failure. I'll let Apple's 2013 WWDC introduction video do the talking on this one (if it isn't taken down).

I mean, given the reporting from folks who have spent many long years in the industry, it seems they forget exactly who they are talking about.

Apple has an untold number of active prototypes in development and magnitudes more in a graveyard out back. I have no doubt that Apple's secret projects division is working on everything from rollable OLED to drones.

That doesn't mean we'll ever see any of these products, nor does it mean that every abandoned prototype is a sign of failure and mismanagement. Every time a project is canceled in spite of the sunk cost, that is a victory.

But apparently three known abandoned internal prototypes are a sign of confusion, failure, and mismanagement.

These are likely three of dozens of prototypes being conceptualized at Apple Park. What is interesting is that instead of fast-tracking one of the other potential designs in the 28-month interval between the M2 model's reveal and the M5 model's launch, Apple stuck with what it had.

Meta VR Glasses are an example of what a compromised product might look like. Lower resolution, lower fidelity, lower field of view — clearly Apple didn't want this even if it could build it.

What's interesting is the "failure" narrative about Apple Vision Pro assumes a lot that we don't know. No one outside of Apple knows the success metric for the product or if Apple is meeting that.

Apple Car is one of Apple's biggest no's

Capturing a quarter of Meta's VR headset revenue in a single holiday quarter in spite of an entrenched market doesn't sound like a failure to me.

Also, CEO John Ternus is apparently supposed to dislike the whole project and has reportedly "put it on ice." Meanwhile, his press tours have revealed only positive talk of the product, insisting that unique use cases like surgeons using the product are why Apple is in this business.

However, the reports want us to view this as a reason to dislike Apple Vision Pro.

Life-changing medical procedures aren't enough, no. We need this thing to sell in the tens of millions to matter.

Even with the Apple Vision Pro team reportedly "on ice" they are busy developing a "revamped" N224 that could be the true successor to Apple Vision Pro. There are about four prototypes being tested, and one that even uses an external compute block like Meta VR Glasses.

Apple didn't pivot, it doubled down on its hardware and spec combination until technology caught up

That's how Meta apparently "beat" Apple to market with a device that doesn't launch until spring at $1,299. Early reports suggest it works fine, but the lack of light shields and more limited field of view and fidelity make it a worse experience.

But of course, Meta apparently "demonstrated" that Apple's execution was the problem all along with the Apple Vision Pro. Yes, that's definitely it, as long as you ignore the successes of the headset, how it has influenced the market, and how Apple Vision Pro was a clear template for Meta's latest hardware.

It wasn't enough that Meta basically cloned visionOS for its Meta Quest line and mixed reality prototypes. Nope, the company even hired former Apple design chief Alan Dye to help nail down that Apple look and feel.

But I'm confused. I thought we were all meant to dislike the guy for Liquid Glass, but now it's apparently Meta's victory for poaching him.

I guess as long as it's a failure for Apple, reporting will choose whatever narrative best fits that mold.

The inconsistent reporting around Apple Vision Pro has been incredible. It's dead, it's not, it's dead again, development is halted, it's going again but on life support.

Apple Vision Pro is the template spatial computing is being built on, but that's still a 'failure' apparently

Analysts and pundits need Apple Vision Pro to fail for whatever reason. That's why every product even close to AR/VR/MR has been deemed an "Apple Vision Pro killer."

Either this thing is dead and a failure, or it's one hell of a resilient product in spite of poor punditry. I think I'll go with the latter until I see the gravestone.

Apple's regular employee churn and reconfigurations internally don't show anything but business as usual. As far as AppleInsider has been able to uncover, development continues, albeit slowly, as Apple waits for technology to catch up with Apple's vision of the next-generation headset.

Remember, Apple Vision Pro's only true problems are its high starting price and lack of developer support. Everything else is just opinion and conjecture.

items.title: Apple Music finally lands in four countries 11 years after launch
items.content_html:
Apple Music is now available in more countries, with iPhone users in Albania and three others now able to subscribe and listen to tracks.

While Apple does strive to get its services available in as many territories as possible, some are slower to gain services than others. On Wednesday, the list of countries Apple Music is available in grew by four.

Initially spotted by @Aaronp613 on X and confirmed by a check of Apple's Media Services page, Apple Music is now available in Albania, Brunei, Burkina Faso, and Pakistan.

The launches occur a mere 11 years after the initial unveiling of Apple Music in over 100 countries back in June 2015.

The additional countries follow after a number of other changes relating to Apple Music took place in the last few weeks. This includes the testing of countdown clocks for upcoming album drops, as well as the opening of the Apple Music Hall in London.

It's not the only Services-related change on Wednesday, either. Apple Pay has also launched in India, after nine years of negotiations.

items.title: More releases, more often will be the Apple way under CEO Ternus
items.content_html:
New CEO John Ternus plans for Apple to speed up product development, with the aim to bring out more products throughout the year instead of a few well-worn events.

Barely a month in the seat, Apple CEO John Ternus is preparing to make big changes to the way the company works. Leaning on his engineering background, he wants Apple to be the same way, working to develop new products at a more rapid rate.

As part of this, Bloomberg reports that Ternus is considering a shake-up to the way that Apple launches products. While everyone is used to the usual fall iPhone events and spring launches, Ternus wants to increase the frequency so it goes throughout the year instead.

Spring and fall launches will probably continue to exist, and will be the focus for the meantime. But expect more introductions at other times of year.

Ternus believes Apple needs to become more experimental and to introduce new products more quickly, unidentified employees told the report. All so that Apple can stay competitive in a market that is so AI-centric.

Employees speaking to the report say that changing such an ingrained development practice will be hard. It's a process that could take years.

The change in tempo for releases is only one of the initiatives Ternus wants to embark on, the report continues.

The company is already starting to cut costs, but Ternus also wants to add more sources of revenue.

The primary form of this is to expand the roster of products and services by developing new offerings for consumers. There's also an interest in generating more revenue from existing product users.

Services has been a long-term source of growth for Apple. But, as that starts to slow down, Apple will need to come up with new ideas to keep it from going flat or edging into decline.

In the short term, Apple has set itself up to sell more to consumers in the coming year. Especially when it comes to products going in new directions.

Aside from the usual suspects, there are the AirPods with cameras, as well as the continually rumored launch of Apple Glass. Another big launch will be the eventual launch of the 20th-anniversary iPhone.

items.title: Thousands of banks can now sue over Apple Pay fees in one antitrust case
items.content_html:
Thousands of U.S. banks and credit unions can pursue their Apple Pay fee claims together after a federal judge certified their antitrust lawsuit as a class action.

The financial institutions accuse Apple of blocking competing tap-to-pay wallets on iPhone while charging card issuers fees for transactions. They argue Apple could impose those fees because rival wallets couldn't compete for contactless payments on the iPhone.

Judge Jeffrey White certified the class on September 23 and rejected Apple's attempt to exclude the plaintiffs' damages expert. The ruling doesn't decide whether Apple violated antitrust law or owes the issuers money.

Card issuers pay Apple 0.15% of the value of credit card purchases made through Apple Pay and half a cent for each debit transaction, according to the credit unions' lawsuit. For example, a $100 credit card purchase through Apple Pay costs the card issuer 15 cents in Apple Pay fees.

Affinity Credit Union, GreenState Credit Union, and Consumers Co-op Credit Union filed the lawsuit in 2022. They argue Apple couldn't have sustained its Apple Pay fees with meaningful competition, pointing to Android wallets that don't charge card issuers transaction fees.

The lawsuit alleges Apple blocked rival wallets from using the iPhone's contactless payment hardware, leaving Apple Pay as the only option for tap-to-pay card transactions. The credit unions say the lack of competition let Apple charge inflated fees, which they want repaid along with changes to the challenged practices.

Apple previously tried to have the case dismissed. A 2023 ruling allowed the monopolization claim to continue while dismissing a separate allegation that Apple unlawfully tied iOS devices to Apple Pay.

The certified class covers U.S. entities that issued an Apple Pay-enabled card and paid Apple a fee for a transaction made with that card. The plaintiffs estimate that thousands of banks and credit unions qualify.

Apple didn't dispute that the proposed class was large enough to meet the numerical requirement for certification. White found that the court can resolve key questions for the entire class rather than separately for every issuer.

The questions include whether Apple had monopoly power, harmed competition, and charged fees that injured card issuers. Apple's uniform rates for credit and debit transactions could also provide a common way to calculate any overcharges if the issuers prove their case.

The ruling also allows Christopher Vellturo, the plaintiffs' damages expert, to testify. Vellturo compares Apple's issuer fees with the zero-dollar issuer fees he attributes to competing mobile wallets, then uses that difference to estimate how much class members may have overpaid.

Apple challenged his methodology and asked the court to exclude his testimony. White instead found that Apple's objections concern how convincing the analysis is, leaving the company free to attack its assumptions and conclusions as the case continues.

Apple's restrictions have changed since the credit unions filed the lawsuit. Starting with iOS 18.1 in 2024, eligible third-party apps can handle contactless iPhone payments without routing them through Apple Pay, and users can choose an eligible app as their default for contactless transactions.

Developers still need Apple's approval and a commercial agreement that includes applicable platform fees, according to Apple's documentation. Apple's developer fees are separate from the Apple Pay transaction fees challenged in the lawsuit.

The September 23 ruling lets the issuers pursue their claims together, including a request to change Apple's practices. Expanded NFC access could affect what changes remain necessary, but it doesn't resolve claims over fees already paid or establish that the fees were unlawful.

items.title: 'Get Ready' to pre-order the iPhone Duo starting October 12
items.content_html:
Apple will let customers set up their iPhone Duo pre-order starting October 12, four days before orders open on October 16.

Apple's first foldable iPhone, known as the iPhone Duo, debuted on September 9, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. While the latter two are already available for purchase, those looking to get an iPhone Duo will have to wait until mid-October 2026.

Pre-orders for iPhone Duo start at 8 AM ET on Friday, October 16, but Apple says its customers can "get ready" for pre-orders starting October 12.

In essence, it will be possible to customize your iPhone Duo even before pre-orders officially open. From October 12 through October 15, you can select your desired accessories, color, carrier, storage option, shipping address, billing address, AppleCare+ plan, and payment method.

Preparing in advance will let you pre-order the iPhone Duo much more quickly, and it might help you acquire the device on its scheduled release day. Given the rumors around limited supply chain output, you'll want every advantage you can get when ordering the iPhone Duo.

Apple says iPhone Duo availability begins on October 23.

items.title: How to watch the Charlie Brown Halloween movie for free
items.content_html:
Join Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus, Lucy, and the rest of the gang and tune in to watch "It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" for free for everybody on Apple TV. Here's how, and when.

For many of us, Charlie Brown and the "Peanuts" gang mark some of our very first movie memories. That's why Apple TV is ensuring everyone can revisit those warm and fuzzy childhood feelings, regardless of whether they have an active Apple TV subscription.

"It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" follows the gang on their Halloween adventures, including trick-or-treating and waiting for the Great Pumpkin.

It's gone from CBS, and PBS, likely forever. But, Apple TV will once again make the Halloween classic available for free to any who want to watch on Saturday, October 17 and Sunday, October 18.

Charlie Brown and the gang will also return for free during the Thanksgiving and Christmas seasons later in 2026.

In 2020, Apple signed a deal with rights holders WildBrain and Peanuts Worldwide to bring Snoopy, Charlie Brown, and the whole gang to Apple TV. In October 2025, the company announced an extension of that deal.

Apple TV holds streaming rights to all Peanuts content through 2030. To watch new or classic specials outside limited streaming windows, you'll need an Apple TV subscription.

Apple TV offers a free, three-month trial when a first-time watcher buys a qualifying device, such as an iPhone. There is also a free seven-day trial, after which the monthly cost is $14.99 or $119.99 per year.

items.title: Small layoffs and budget cuts are hitting Apple, with more expected
items.content_html:
New Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly planning layoffs ranging from small-scale ones in large teams, but also cancelling projects.

Apple has recently laid off some staff from Apple Vision Pro development, but a new report says that employees across the company are expecting more serious numbers of redundancies to come. According to Bloomberg, it's a result of new CEO Ternus aiming to cut costs and focus on developing fewer products.

The report also claims, though, that some of the layoffs were linked to employee performance. So at least some of the layoffs appear to be more due to efficiency than to budget cutting.

At the same time, Ternus is said to be canceling some projects that are early in their development. He's believed to be doing this in order to focus on changing how often Apple releases new and updated products.

Canceling projects is likely to mean layoffs, but it's not clear when or really whether these cuts will happen, though. That's because the report also cites Ternus cancelling a plan to lay off around 5,000 AppleCare customer service staff.

It had been expected that AI would be able to perform some of their tasks, but Apple is said to have put these plans on hold.

The expectation that more layoffs are coming is more because of changes to budgets. Reportedly some Apple divisions had been led to expect budget and headcount increases in 2027, but those are now not going to happen.

That does not mean there won't be any increase in budget, but it's said that the headcount is being kept flat. That typically means no recruitment and at most only replacing people who leave or are redeployed.

There have reportedly been a small number of layoffs in Apple Fitness+. But given how that service retains its main costs such as studio space, that is more likely to be refocusing what the service provides rather than saving money.

items.title: Hong Kong police want Apple's help in stopping $3.8M iPhone 18 Pro fraud
items.content_html:
Since the iPhone 18 Pro went on sale, police in Hong Kong have dealt with over 1,500 cases of buyers using suspicious credit cards. They think Apple can stop it.

Hong Kong criminals have been involved in international theft before, and the Apple's progress in China at least initially faced bribery and fraud. Now according to local news site The Standard, fraudsters are targeting the iPhone 18 Pro by buying it in bulk using fake credit cards.

They're doing it to the tune of 1,503 reported suspicious charges on credit cards since the iPhone 18 Pro went on sale. The charges amounted to over $3.82 million, but the local police say that they have had all of these transactions canceled.

Significantly, Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming told Kowloon City district council that in each case Apple's online security and verification were not in effect. Without explanation, he attributes the issue to what is being called a loophole in Apple's online store.

"This meant that one-time passwords or mobile app verification were not required," he told the South China Morning Post, "allowing fraudsters to place large orders using illegally obtained credit card information."

It's claimed that Apple's identity and payment verification requirements were somehow waived for web purchases. The fraudsters used VPNs and provided false or incomplete addresses.

Apple would subsequently email to ask for clarification over the delivery address, and the criminals would now specify a public location.

Chow also said that the police had asked Apple to review its transaction processes to prevent such fraud. He noted that the iPhone Duo is due to launch in October, suggesting he expects another rise in fraud attempts.

Apple has not commented publicly. They likely won't.

items.title: Apple Creator Studio lets you change iPhone 18 Pro video focus after filming
items.content_html:
Apple Creator Studio's latest updates add selection tools to Pixelmator Pro for iPad, new editing options for iPhone 18 Pro video, and changes across its productivity apps.

It's time to update Apple Creator Studio. The latest release touches nearly every app in the collection, from video and image editing to presentations and spreadsheets.

Pixelmator Pro for iPad now has Select and Mask controls for refining selections around difficult edges, such as hair and fur. On Mac and iPad, the app also gains sports, business, and podcast artwork templates.

Final Cut Pro and Motion on Mac can apply Cinematic mode effects to video captured natively on iPhone 18 Pro. In Final Cut Pro, editors can change focus points and depth of field directly in the timeline.

Compressor can convert footage with the new Cinematic mode effects to the previous Cinematic mode format. It also adds HEVC and MPEG-4 export presets designed for sharing projects on social media.

Subscribers also get new templates and themes in Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. Keynote's Apple Intelligence-powered slide generation can now create images for a presentation.

All three iWork apps let users request access to shared files. Pages for Mac adds a reading and writing Screen View, and Numbers gains trigonometry, statistics, and logic functions.

Freeform boards now adapt to Dark Mode, while folders help organize boards and invite collaborators. Users can also request access to shared boards and add content through Shortcuts.

Apple Intelligence Writing Tools can rewrite, proofread, and summarize handwritten notes. In visionOS 27, users can pull board items into their space and view 3D models together.

Launched in January, Apple Creator Studio is a collection of creative and productivity apps. It lies somewhere between Adobe's Creative Cloud creative suite and Microsoft 365's productivity apps.

Apple Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year. New users can score a one-month free trial.

Education pricing drops it even lower, to $2.99 per month or $29.99 per year.

items.title: Variable aperture iPhone 18 Pro now supported by Final Cut Camera
items.content_html:
The latest update to Final Cut Camera for iOS can take advantage of the iPhone 18 Pro variable aperture system, giving video professionals more control over the shot.

Final Cut Camera is a companion app for Final Cut Pro for iPad, enabling users to capture live multi-camera projects with a collection of iPhones, as well as for more conventional filming purposes. In an update rolling out on Tuesday, the app is being upgraded with new features.

The big and timely change is variable aperture support for the new Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro. Final Cut Camera can now select one of the available apertures from f1.48 to F4, with users also able to choose shutter or aperture priority modes, when recording video.

There's also Cinematic mode effects for other video recordings, including those recorded in ProRes and Apple Log.

The update also introduces support for video scopes,, including the RGB parade and histogram. False color and clipping indicators with threshold settings are also available for dialing in the exposure.

Professional shooters can also get a clean video signal for broadcast-quality streams using an HDMI-to-SDI converter.

There's also the capability to set a genlock frame delay, so that you can compensate for image artifacts from a record display. More usefully, this can also help deal with latency differences with other genlocked cameras.

The update to Final Cut Camera is free, as is the app, and requires iOS 26.66 or later.

items.title: M5 Max Mac Studio review: Better choice than Ultra for most desks
items.content_html:
There are some interesting choices to make, if you're looking at buying a 2026 Mac Studio. There is one clear choice for Mac-centric workflows, and one for a AI powerhouse.

Despite the drama on the Internet about the Mac Studio, Apple has always had $5000+ computers to sell you. The 2026 Mac Studio lineup is not an exception, but rather an exemplar.

There was the Mac IIfx, way back in the day, and much later the original Mac Pro, which after starting at $2499 got expensive quickly to well over $5000 in 2006 dollars, for just a little more power at each step. There's the iMac Pro, and so forth.

The Mac Studio has that $5499 Ultra starting model. That's a big jump over the $2499 M5 Max Mac studio. That one is aimed not so much at the Mac loyal, but to the AI bros, looking for a compact and power-efficient form factor, no matter the cost.

As such, the Mac Studio M5 Ultra model is the headline-grabber for the sheer amount of power on tap, but it is not the best thing to come out of the refresh. That M5 Ultra is extremely expensive, overkill for just about any actual Mac-based workload, and as of September 29, 2026, unavailable until 2027.

What you can get now, and has a far better price-to-performance ratio is the M5 Max Mac Studio.

And, it's now my daily driver, like the M1 Ultra was before it.

This is a very expensive practical demonstration of "If it ain't broke..."

The Mac Studio design carries over unchanged. It is a compact aluminum block that sits on a desk.

Mac Studio review: In its packaging

This isn't a disappointment, but more the reality of how Apple designs products. Apple likes that five or six-year product iteration between major redesigns, and we're on year four of the Mac Studio.

As it has been since 2022, it measures 7.7 inches square and 3.7 inches tall, and weighs in at six pounds. There's the massive vent on the back, the circular vented plinth underneath, and the usual selection and placement of ports.

For the M5 Max Mac Studio there are two 10-gigabit USB-C ports and an SDXC card slot on the front, as well as a small status light. On the back is the Thunderbolt 5, USB-A, power, and Ethernet ports, the same as it has been since the advent of the line.

Mac Studio review: A top-down view

And that design, with the massive heat sink that occupies about 70% of the interior volume of the enclosure, is what allows the Mac Studio to be very quiet, even when getting hammered. I've already stressed the hell out of this machine, and in a 36 DBa office, it never got above 39 DBa, using my faithful Kanomax meter that I've had for years.

The M5 Max is the heart of this machine. My unit that I bought for my own personal use is on review here, with 36GB of RAM, an upgraded 1TB SSD, an 18-core CPU and a 32-core GPU. There are more options, extending the pricing ladder to more than the M5 Ultra version.

Apple splits the CPU into 6 super cores and 12 performance cores, with the usual platitudes about clock speed.

This is usually where we discuss speed, but this time, we have to also talk about AI.

A 16-core Neural Engine handles machine learning duties as usual, but it's not the only thing. The bigger change is in the GPU.

Each of those GPU cores now has a Neural Accelerator, which helps with AI tasks.

This is a massive change for machine learning workloads. Sure, the M5 Ultra has up to GPU 80 cores to play with and two Neural Engines, but there's a lot in the base M5 Max configuration to shout about for far less cash.

As reviewed, memory bandwidth is 460GB/s for the base configuration. The 40-core GPU option raises it to 614GB/s, if you opt to pay more. .

Geekbench Single-core results

When it comes to the single-core test from Geekbench 7, the M5 Max at 3,718 demonstrates how Apple's cores get faster over time. While the M3 Ultra has a lot more CPU cores, it doesn't help at all for a test focused on one fast core.

Geekbench Multi-core results

The multi-core test is a much closer race because of the difference in core counts. The M5 Max is still first, with its 18-core CPU and fast cores achieving 35,104 in our testing.

That said, the M3 Ultra is narrowly behind, with a Geekbench 7 figure of 35,056. While the M3 Ultra doesn't have the core speed, it makes up the difference by having a massive 28 cores in the lower-tier chip variant.

Geekbench Metal results

For Metal, it's a fairly similar story of core performance versus sheer quantity. The M5 Max's 32-core GPU secures the win with 238,404.

That said, the M3 Ultra model with a 64-core GPU, double the core count, still manages an impressive 225,725. The extra cores of the 80-core GPU M3 Ultra could even the race out, or even give it a slight lead, but not when we're comparing the base level of chip families.

To further test out the new Mac Studio's chips, we used the same tasks we used to shake down the Mac Pro, when it had the M2 chip, as well as the last generation of Intel Mac Pro.

We've been using these tests with the help of some people I've known for decades. While I don't have a peek under the hood, I've been told that there haven't been notable improvements in the code since before we started using them for Pro hardware testing.

One workflow is the simulation of a fluid flowing over a moving body, such as a boat hull. This is a calculation-heavy task that doesn't use the GPU much, and the test was carried out using Intel-native code and is still, in 2026, using Rosetta on the Apple Silicon hardware.

For the next batch of Pro hardware, this will be Apple Silicon-native code, but it isn't yet.

Complex Fluid Flow over a Moving Body results

At 5 minutes and 12 seconds, the improvement in the M5 Max continue to be steady. We are now almost at a third of the time of the Intel Mac Pro.

A second fluid simulation test is a design tool that simulates water and steam flowing through a complex engineered system, incorporating heat transfers to the tenth of a degree, and fluid flows. This time, it remains Apple Silicon-native code, and the system simulated has remained the same for the last ten years.

This is a GPU-heavy task.

Complex Fluid Flow Through Piping results

At 6 minutes and 18 seconds, there's more improvement here again, this time with a much bigger chunk of time taken off from the M3 Ultra and M4 Max's figures.

The stoichiometry test is a complex chemical equilibrium reaction calculation and simulation, involving interactions and reactions between organic compounds and inorganic ones. Again, this is Apple Silicon-native code. It does leverage the GPU cores some, but is more CPU-bound.

Chemistry Stoichiometry Reaction Calculation and Simulation performance

The time of just 32 seconds is a massive cut from both the M3 Ultra and M4 Max's 46 seconds and 44 seconds. It's almost half the M2 Mac Pro's speed too, and just a ninth of the Intel model.

This Xcode test is a compilation of the application used for the Stoichiometry test. This is an especially useful test for developers.

Xcode compile test performance

Here, the M5 Max Mac Studio hits a new milestone for this particular test, getting below a minute for the first time. That 51 seconds is also less than half the times of the M3 Ultra and M4 Max and less than a third of the M2 Mac Pro.

The Image Enhancement and Identification test uses involves high-altitude image processing, and the identification of subjects of interest on the ground. This is drawn from a 3TB database stored on an internal SSD.

The code is both Apple Silicon native and leverages the GPU heavily, plus Apple's Video Toolkit.

Image Enhancement and Identification performance

The 2 minutes and 4 seconds of the M5 Max model is very good, especially when viewed against the previous Max and Ultra models.

Against more historic models, namely the Intel Mac Pro with and without Afterburner, the M5 Max is a breath of fresh air.

The timing of the tasks is more than just a mathematical interpretation of gains or losses in simulated workflows based on synthetic workflows. We like Geekbench a lot for general performance assessment, but it doesn't hold a candle to running your own code on new hardware and seeing what's faster.

We highly, highly recommend doing just that, before you drop cash on Mac Studios.

As I said before, my unit shipped with 36GB of unified memory. That is the standard amount for the M5 Max at the base tier with 36 GPU cores, and the only one you can choose with this chip.

You can go to higher levels if you want, but you will have to opt for the upper-tier chip. If you do, you instead start at 48GB and have 48GB and 128GB capacities available.

Mac Studio review: The front ports are still useful, if not Thunderbolt 5.

For storage, you could opt for a base 512GB capacity, which is extremely small in this day and age.
