You can go higher, upgrading to 1TB, 2TB, 4TB, and 8TB. A 16TB capacity is available for those paying the big bucks for the Ultra version.

With the 1TB version, I was practically seeing 10 gigabyte per second read and write speeds.

I do have access to the 512GB storage model, which is a different story. Read speeds hit a peak of about 6.4 gigabytes per second, but write speeds were notably worse at about 5.1 gigabytes per second.

This all comes down to parallelization. I suspect that the 512GB model has a single slotted and theoretically upgradeable SSD module, while the 1TB version has two.

I'm not quite ready to rip open my own machine and find out, but the teardowns will be available soon enough.

Connectivity is a strength of the Mac Studio. The rear carries four Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gbps, so long as you have the hardware that supports it.

Along with the front USB-C ports, there's also a pair of USB-A at the back, as well as HDMI 2.1, 10Gb Ethernet, and a headphone jack.

Thankfully, Apple has still retained the power button at the rear. The Mac mini power button location is a mistake.

Mac Studio review: The rear port view

The only real issue here is, as always, Apple's decision to make the front ports USB-C, connecting at 10Gb/s. You can get them to be 120Gb/s Thunderbolt 5, but only if you pony up for Ultra.

There's not a lot to say here that isn't already known. The Thunderbolt 5 ports on this Mac Studio are just as fast as they are on the M5 Max MacBook Pro, and the M4 Max Mac Studio.

Expect more of the same.

The M5 Max drives up to five external displays. That can be up to four 6K 60Hz screens and a fifth 5K 60Hz, or four 4K 165Hz with the fifth 5K 60Hz again.

If you want to go all-out, there's the ability to have two 8K 60Hz screens or two 5K 120Hz panels, or even 4K 20Hz, with a third 5K 60Hz over HDMI.

If you have the displays that support it, you can have up to four displays running off a single Thunderbolt 4 port.

Mac Studio review: It definitely runs with one screen, but you can go large with three of them...

Audio-wise, you have HDMI multi-channel audio support, the 3.5mm headphone jack with high-impedance headphone support, and the built-in speaker.

Wireless moves forward this year too. The Mac Studio now has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, through the use of the N1 chip.

Lastly, if you have a smart home, you can take advantage of Thread.

The main advantage here, and improvement, is the Wi-Fi 7. But, if you're using Wi-Fi on a Mac Studio for workloads, you must be doing so because you have to.

Wire your work networks. Speed is more consistent, and better, than Wi-Fi will be. And, 10Gbit networks are getting cheaper by the day.

For the AI workloads, there's always direct Thunderbolt connections for properly-coded models. More on this in the Mac Studio Ultra review in October, and in a project we're doing now rack mounting two in a portable enclosure.

The Mac Studio comes in two forms. This M5 Max sits obviously below the pricier M5 Ultra.

The Max suits most professional and creative work. The Ultra targets huge memory needs and eight-display setups.

At $2,499 to start, the M5 Max is the "bargain" choice. The Ultra begins at $5,499, more than double.

For most nearly every Mac Studio buyer with work to do, the M5 Max is the sensible pick. Only the heaviest AI workloads justify the Ultra.

My main Mac, up until the M5 Max Mac Studio, was the M1 Ultra Mac Studio. I got it at a Woot sale, about three years ago for a song.

I sold it in the beginning of July. Selling that 64GB of RAM stock in my older machine, coupled with my military discount, funded the entire purchase.

Fortunately for my desk, and my wall mount, the M5 Max Mac Studio changes nothing on the outside. All the upgrades are inside the same small case.

Mac Studio review: Vent holes in the circular foot assist the main rear vent in circulating air for cooling.

The gains that matter are the chip and the storage. Faster silicon and AI capabilities headline the update.

Our unit adds 1TB of storage to the standard build. That is a sensible step up for real project files, and real workflows, beyond just benchmarks.

For pro users in the Apple ecosystem, it's a safe upgrade. If time is money, this outperforms, handily, your M1 Ultra Mac Studio. It's time to upgrade.

I very rarely give out perfect scores, but I have here. The original M1 Max Mac Studio was less expensive, sure, but in late 2026, the fact that this much Mac workstation power starts at $2499 remains impressive.

I've also been using the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. The scores for the workflows weren't much different, and in one case slower. More on that in about a month, because there is no way that a week of review time is enough for that one.

And besides, unless you find one at retail, it's going to be months before you can use it.

The M5 Max is gettable today, with a far better price to performance ratio at about 90%+ the practical power for Mac desktop workflows versus the M5 Ultra. That latter machine has a specific point, and a very specific user base, though, which we will talk about soon enough.

Apple's 2026 Mac Studio is already on sale, with the standard M5 Max/36GB RAM/512GB SSD spec discounted to $2,449 at Amazon at the time of this review.

You can compare prices on models with additional storage, RAM, and even the M5 Ultra chip in our 2026 Mac Studio Price Guide, which is updated throughout the day.

items.title: Safety concerns forced ICEblock removal, Apple tells lawmaker
items.content_html:
Apple has doubled down on its claims that removing ICEblock and similar apps from the App Store was necessary for safety, though chiefly because it was never going to admit to bowing to government pressure.

In July 2025, the Department of Justice publicly threatened the developer of ICEblock, an app that let users say when Immigration and Enforcement Officers were spotted in an area. The app was intended to help people avoid trouble spots, such as the riots caused when ICE agents entered Los Angeles against the city mayor's orders.

Apple is now being asked to justify how in October 2025, it subsequently removed ICEblock from the App Store. Only excerpts of Apple's latest comments have been reported, but CNN says that the company's July 2026 letter doubled down on safety as the reason for the removal.

The letter, written in response to Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) of the House Judiciary Committee, reportedly says that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had "expressed serious concerns to Apple that ICEBlock posed a threat to the safety of federal officers."

This had been followed by FBI Director Kash Patel claiming that apps such a ICEblock had been used to track agents. That statement was specifically about a shooting at an ICE facility in September 2025, which wasn't related to the ICEBlock app, given that the building obviously wasn't in motion, and was known as an ICE facility for over a decade.

Apple also says that it saw a "significant increase in ICE activity and threats against ICE" around this time.

Therefore, says Apple, it decided to remove ICEblock and similar apps. Apple does not say that it was ordered to remove the apps, and the DOJ has previously denied issuing any such order. Our research at the time found that there was no legal order, likely to skirt First Amendment arguments since it wasn't a legal request.

Apple says instead that it concluded that ICE-tracking apps were in violation of App Store policies since they gave users "precise location information about ICE officers (and, as a result, other individuals who may be in proximity to ICE agents, such as protestors or detainees), thus providing a potential roadmap for targeted violence and creating a significant risk of harm."

Apple's removal of ICEblock prompted Portland protesters to march on Apple Stores dressed as Santa Claus. Image source: keir-pdx on Bluesky

The published excerpts from the letter continue with Apple saying that it "does not take decisions about removing apps from the App Store lightly, but acts when it must — especially when there are serious concerns that an app is creating safety risks."

ICEblock did not induce violence against agents, but the DOJ and FBI said that it did. After they said that, Apple removed the apps.

Apple will of course never say that it bowed to government pressure. But it appears to be solely repeating the safety argument that Rep. Raskin in his initial letter to the company refused to accept.

Raskin had pointed out that the September 2025 shooter "did not need a tracking app to locate the fixed position of a government building." According to Raskin, the shooter had also been "reported to have found the address using an app that comes standard on Apple devices," and which was not removed.

"Monitoring the actions of federal immigration authorities who have been deployed to (users') neighborhoods, is a core First Amendment right and not a crime," Raskin said.

The questions that Raskin first asked Apple can be read in full online. He began investigating both Apple and Google back in February 2026, and his later letter required detailed explanations of what apps were removed and why.

Apple has not commented publicly. The DOJ has also not spoken about Raskin's letter or Apple's response, but it has continued to claim that ICE apps are dangerous.

"Our law officers are facing an over 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats," said a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson. "Further, these apps are a method to interfere with law enforcement activities and harbor illegal aliens."

ICEblock and similar apps are not illegal, in the same way that Apple Maps pinpointing speed traps is not illegal. The DHS has not commented on reasons why alleged assaults against ICE agents are up, it has only targeted apps.

And, locations were generally after-the-fact data. User reports tended towards where ICE action was, not is, and lagged a half-hour or more behind actual movements.

Given that Apple's response to Raskin has not been published fully, it's not clear what else the company may have said. It isn't known whether Raskin will consider the matter closed, nor yet what steps he or the House Judiciary Committee could take next.

But what Apple must be hoping will happen next is that the whole issue be forgotten. Apple can say it wasn't ordered to remove the apps, and the DOJ can say it never made such an order, but effectively that is what happened.

Apple will remove apps that are against the law, and ICEBlock is not. This time, it bowed to government pressure and given the the administration's willingness to punish companies on a whim, it is understandable.

But it's also an abdication of Apple's stated morals on free speech for individuals.

items.title: Apple's haptic feedback $5.7B trial loss likely to get pared way back
items.content_html:
Lawyers for the winning side, Taction Technology, say that they expect Apple to negotiate the loss down and so also cut back the law firm's profits. How terrible for them.

Apple was found guilty of infringing the patents of Taction Technology in its Taptic Engine, as used in the Apple Watch and many more devices, with a jury awarding damages of over $5.7 billion. In case anyone thought the lawyers did this one pro bono, legal firm Burford Capital says that it ought to be paid $1.4 billion.

According to Reuters, this win has sent the legal firm's US stock up over 6%. But Burford Capital has now cautioned that it is unlikely to receive the full sum.

That's not because Taction Technology won't pay up, it's because the sum itself is likely to be greatly reduced. Burford Capital initially says that any large award will typically get watered down during post-trial proceedings such as appeals.

It then notes, though, that this particular verdict faces significant risks. Burford Capital suspects that both Apple and Taction Technology will ultimately agree to settle for an unspecified but considerably reduced sum.

Burford Capital may be just managing expectations. Or it could be looking for sympathy that it's not very likely to get. It's possible, though, that this is based on an appreciation of how good Apple's lawyers are, or perhaps that there is an as-yet unrevealed weakness in the case.

For example, the jury's verdict was that Apple did infringe on the patents, for instance, but also that it did not do so knowingly. Apple continues to maintain that it disagrees with the verdict, and that the awarded sum was not based on any evidence. So, there's that appeal which ultimately might mean that the lawyers get nothing.

Taptic Technology first filed its suit against Apple back in April 2021. Apple subsequently won the case in the US District Court for the Southern District of California, but then in 2025 that verdict was overturned by the Federal Circuit.

The Federal Circuit found that the original trial improperly struck expert testimony. That original trial was also said to have unfairly limited Taptic Technology's claims.

Consequently, the case went back to court and into a new jury trial. It is this trial that saw Apple hit with $5.7 billion damages, and which it now says it will appeal

So this result has already been a long time coming, but the case will continue for some years yet. After all, it's not really an Apple patent trial if it doesn't extend for multiple years.

items.title: How to escape Photoshop's clutches by installing PhotoGimp
items.content_html:
If you don't want keep paying Adobe, switch to Gimp. Here's how to make Gimp have a user interface very similar to Photoshop with PhotoGimp.

The creative industry is a heavy user of Adobe's Creative Cloud, with it a staple in production houses and studios around the world. Photoshop is one of the many tools within that package, and is widely used within design and photography fields.

However, while the world runs on Photoshop, not everyone wants to keep paying a hefty monthly fee for access to the entire bundle. Indeed, even the single-app subscription is a bit steep.

For users wanting to get out of Adobe's subscription, they have to look at alternative options. There's certainly a lot of them out there, but it reveals an entirely new problem.

If you switch apps, you have to learn how to use it.

Sure, on Mac and iPadOS, there's Procreate, Pixelmator Pro, and many other art tools to purchase and use, often at a lower cost compared to Adobe's packages. If you do switch, you face a period of time where you have to relearn what you could do on Photoshop, but in an entirely different user interface.

Then there's the sheer number of keyboard shortcuts that seasoned Photoshop pros will have committed to muscle memory. A lot of the shortcuts, especially those for rarely-used functions, will be different.

It will take time to get back up to speed, which to some could be too high a cost for moving over from Photoshop.

PhotoGimp is a potential answer for people wanting to switch to the completely free Gimp, referring to the GNU Image Manipulation Program.

Aside from having a fun name, Gimp is a cross-platform image editor that is free to use on macOS, Windows, and Linux. While it is a powerful tool, it's also open-source, so you can check out and change the source code if you wish.

While free, the attractively priced software has the same problem as others, in that the interface is different from Photoshop. All of the icons are in different places versus the typical Photoshop layout, meaning you will have to take time to learn where everything is.

Photoshop's default layout [left], PhotoGimp's reworking of Gimp's interface [right]

PhotoGimp, on the other hand, solves that problem by being a patch for Gimp. Specifically, one intended to be used by Photoshop users.

Rather than relearning a new interface, PhotoGimp instead changes the interface for you. While not necessarily a 1-to-1 match to Photoshop, it reconfigures Gimp so that the layout and tools are put in a way that mimics Photoshop's placements.

It doesn't stop there, as it can also do keyboard shortcuts, too. The shortcuts in the PhotoGimp patch match those of Windows users of Photoshop, except you map the Windows Control key usage for Command.

To be clear, this doesn't suddenly turn Gimp into a perfect copy of Photoshop. What the patch does is cut down how much you have to search around and relearn the interface, but it won't change how Gimp's functions actually work.

It's not a silver bullet, but it does help traverse the knowledge and muscle memory gap.

The process is relatively simple, but does require you to access the Application Support folder within the Library in your Mac's user directory.

After installing Gimp, make an immediate backup of the related folder in Application Support, since PhotoGimp replaces many files in it. You could always uninstall Gimp and start from scratch, but making a backup of the folder would save a bit of time and effort.

The process of installing Gimp for Mac

If the patch has been applied successfully, you'll see a different loading screen for PhotoGimp, followed by a fairly familiar layout.

At this point, you can proceed with trying out a free alternative to Photoshop, without needing to think too hard about finding the main tools and features.

items.title: Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation - excellent price for a storage dock
items.content_html:
At about $330, the Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation adds fast storage, multiple display support, and 140W charging to your new Mac. It's pretty nice, but not perfect.

It was Apple's choice to switch to (almost) all USB-C in 2016. They really haven't reversed course on this, other than conceding that MagSafe was pretty good, and so is native HDMI.

So, if you're a regular AppleInsider reader, you know there's a dock for everybody. Orico is relatively new to this game, but to date, what we've seen from them in the Thunderbolt 5 Dock is pretty solid, with a good price point to boot.

The dock uses an aluminum alloy body with plastic accents. It is compact and light at 0.85 pounds.

It is built to sit on a desk beside a Mac. The silver finish suits an Apple setup.

The M.2 slot sits inside the enclosure. A drive installs without extra cables.

Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation review: Front port view

The problem with all this is that it is very, very hot. While running with the SSD, the unit's surface temperature hits about 111F. This is not enough to burn, but it's also not comfortable to the touch.

We didn't have any connectivity problems, but we're concerned about long-term stability. This is an odd one where we get to keep the product after review instead of returning it to the vendor, so we'll get back to you on this.

One Thunderbolt 5 port connects to the host Mac. It runs at up to 80Gbps, delivering up to 140W of power to the host computer. In our testing that is enough to supply a 16-inch MacBook Pro under load, and supply a very small charge to the battery while getting hammered.

Two more Thunderbolt 5 ports face outward. They connect peripherals or daisy-chain up to six devices.

Older Macs still work, but slower. A Thunderbolt 4 or 3 Mac drops to its own ceiling, and monitor support will change based on the host, and the available bandwidth.

Speeds are about as you'd expect. We didn't see any issues with external peripherals here. Power is sufficient for external drives, and so forth. It is not enough for Apple's SuperDrive, through.

The dock's standout feature is its internal drive bay. It takes one M.2 NVMe 2280 SSD, which is not provided.

Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation review: The M.2 compartment

Orico says the slot supports PCIe 5.0 drives. It measured speeds up to 6000 megabytes per second. We got about 5200 megabytes per second, which is close enough.

Real speed is gated by Thunderbolt bandwidth, not the drive. Even so, that is fast storage.

The dock offers several ways to add displays. There is one HDMI port and one DisplayPort.

Each does 8K at 30Hz on its own. Together they drop to 4K at 60Hz.

The two Thunderbolt 5 outputs handle displays too. They reach 8K at 60Hz or 4K at 240Hz.

Orico lists support for up to five monitors. This is where Mac buyers must be careful.

Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation review: From above, with the power brick.

Apple Silicon limits how many external displays a Mac drives. Base chips support far fewer than Pro or Max chips.

For example, the M4 MacBook Air drives only two external displays. The five-display figure needs an M4 Max or better.

So check your Mac's display limit before buying for multi-monitor use. This is not a DisplayLink driver dock, so you're limited by the host.

The remaining ports cover everyday needs. There are three USB-A ports at 10Gbps. A single USB-C data port adds another 10Gbps connection. A 2.5GbE jack handles wired networking.

An SD 4.0 and TF 4.0 reader round things out. Both can be read at the same time, which is a nice touch.

A 3.5mm combo jack covers headsets. The bundled adapter supplies 180 watts.

They all work the way you think they will, even when slammed with I/O. The card readers top out at about 280 megabytes per second, each, which is about the same speed as Apple's offering.

The concept behind the Orico Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation is about as simple as it gets. It combines a Thunderbolt 5 hub with fast internal storage.

For a new Mac Studio or MacBook Pro and existing exorbitant SSD prices from Apple, that is useful. One cable adds ports, storage, and 140W charging. Done.

At about $330, it is priced well against big-name rivals. The internal and fast SSD slot is a standout.

Still, though, with that drive installed, I'm very concerned about the heat. Nothing I've ever tested has been this hot externally. More on that in a few months.

I want to like the Orico Thunderbolt 5 dock more than I do. It's a good dock, it has enough ports, it has enough speed, but that external casing is extremely hot.

As part of my longer-term assessment, beyond the month I've already used it, I'll be keeping a close eye on that. If it remains stable, the score will go up. If it doesn't, well...

The Orico Thunderbolt 5 Dock is available from Amazon at a base price of $399.99, with a 20% discount at checkout bringing it down to $319.99.

items.title: First granular 27.0.1 updates arrive for IOS, macOS
items.content_html:
The first granular updates to Apple's milestone operating system releases have arrived, with 27.0.1 updates now here for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, and visionOS.

Apple released its major yearly operating system revision on September 14, bringing iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS to the 27 generation. Two weeks later, Apple's released the first small update to the public.

The granular update is a minor version change, and is quite typical for Apple to release shortly after the main releases.

The new updates are:

Apple also released granular updates to its earlier operating systems, too.

At this early stage, it is unclear exactly what has changed with each operating system. However, while a granular release doesn't tend to have major feature changes, they usually include bug fixes and performance improvements for issues that emerge after launch.

This will probably include fixes for things like Neural Engine timeouts and Face ID kernel panics. For the latter, Apple confirmed a software update will fix the issue.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: The best iPhone for about a month
items.content_html:
In any other year, I'd find a novel way to say that the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the best iPhone ever. While that's true at the time of writing, it's probably only going to be that for a vanishingly small amount of time.

This year is the first where the iPhone Pro Max isn't the most exciting model in Apple's lineup. That honor goes to the iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable device and one that won't hit store shelves until weeks after this review is published. And that leaves me at something of a disadvantage.

If you're reading this after Friday, October 23, 2026, you already know how the iPhone Duo stacks up. Early reviews will be out, and early adopters will have their new phones in their pockets.

There's no denying the iPhone Duo's shadow leaves the iPhone 18 Pro Max in an unusual position. For a few weeks, it sits atop the iPhone lineup, with a premium price point and top-tier features.

And the truth is, it'll still have those post-Duo. The arrival of the foldable iPhone won't make the iPhone 18 Pro Max any less of a stellar device. And let there be no doubt about it: this is every bit the flagship iPhone.

But no matter how good the display is, how impressive the A20 Pro might be, or how long its battery lasts, I can't tell you whether or not you should buy it. I don't even know if it's the best iPhone for me right now.

However, what I can tell you is that the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the best iPhone Pro Max ever. Let me explain why.

The design of any new iPhone is always the first thing you notice, and it's no different with the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Unfortunately, that means you also notice that it looks very familiar indeed.

The new burgundy iPhone 18 Pro

At first blush, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is identical to the iPhone 17 Pro Max that was released a year prior. At 6.43 inches tall, 3.07 inches wide, and 0.34 inches deep, the two share the same dimensions. It's a hair heavier at 8.78 ounces compared to the 17 Pro Max's 8.22 ounces.

The aluminum unibody design is maintained, this time with 40% recycled metal. But the two-tone finish on the rear is gone, replaced by a seamless unified matte finish. Apple chose to make the glass match the metal this time around.

The colors have changed this time out, too. Out is the stunning Cosmic Orange of the iPhone 17 Pro lineup, with Deep Blue following it through the door. In come Burgundy, Glacier Blue, and Black to join the existing Silver option.

There's a design change on the inside, too, with Apple revamping the iPhone's vapor chamber. The aim is to help the new A20 Pro chip (more on that later) stay cool for longer.

Back to the exterior, the iPhone 18 Pro Max still features the large camera area we've become accustomed to. Perhaps "large" doesn't do it justice, but it does at least mean the iPhone 18 Pro Max doesn't wobble when on a table.

Moving around the edges, the iPhone 18 Pro Max maintains the same layout as its predecessor. That means you'll find the power and Camera Control button on the right, the volume and Action Button on the left, and a USB-C port on the bottom.

That USB-C port offers fast USB 3 data transfer speeds of up to 10 Gbps. Charging is faster this time around, bumping the maximum speed up to the 45W mark when paired with a suitable charging brick. The iPhone 17 Pro Max topped out at around 40W.

Finally, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is IP68-rated, as has become the norm. That means it's capable of surviving up to 30 minutes underwater at up to six meters depth.

You know what you're going to get from an iPhone Pro Max, and that's the biggest display of the lineup. This year that means a 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR display, just as it did last year.

Running through the most important specifications, the display has a 2868 x 1320 resolution for a pixel density of 460 pixels per inch. It has a typical peak brightness of 1,000 nits, which increases to 3,000 nits outdoors when the need arises.

This is also a ProMotion display, meaning it has a variable refresh rate from 1Hz to 120Hz for buttery smooth scrolling. It also helps to avoid tearing and other weirdness with fast-paced games.

Like the iPhone 17 Pro Max, the 18 Pro Max sports Apple's Ceramic Shield 2 finish and an anti-reflective coating. The latter means it's easier to see what's on-screen under bright lights. The former should help prevent day-to-day scratches.

One area where the 18 Pro Max does differ from the outgoing model is its Dynamic Island. The change also impacts another important feature in the form of Face ID.

This year, Apple has placed the infrared sensor used for Face ID behind the display. In previous years, a hole was cut in the display to allow infrared light in.

Now, the sensor sits behind a row of display pixels with some of the sub-pixels removed to allow infrared light to pass through. Other pixels around the area have been made brighter to compensate. The effect is that the sensor is invisible to the naked eye.

Thankfully, it also doesn't seem to have impacted performance. Face ID continues to work as it always has, unlocking the iPhone 18 Pro Max just as quickly and reliably as the iPhone Air I've been using the last 12 months.

Moving the infrared sensor means the iPhone 18 Pro Max now has a smaller Dynamic Island as standard. But it also means that it can now display up to three Live Activities simultaneously. It won't change anyone's life, but it's a welcome feature regardless.

For many, buying the Pro iPhones is all about getting the best cameras. That's no different in 2026, with Apple bringing its best camera features to the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has three rear cameras, two of them the same as the ones found on the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

That means buyers will get a 48-megapixel telephoto camera with a 4x optical zoom. That's paired with a 48-megapixel ultra wide camera. Up front, there's an 18-megapixel Center Stage camera for selfies.

But the 48-megapixel Fusion Main camera is where the new magic happens.

48-megapixel Fusion Main camera

We'll cut to the chase. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the first variable aperture to ever find its way to an Apple smartphone. And Apple is making a big deal about it.

Apple's physical mechanical aperture has four settings: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. It defaults to f/1.8, which just so happens to be almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro Max's fixed f/1.78 aperture.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: The main camera rarely disappoints

As photographers will no doubt tell you, the aperture of a camera dictates how much light is allowed into its sensor. The sensor captures the image, so giving it more or less light will change the resulting image in any given situation.

For that reason, allowing as much light into the sensor as possible is obviously beneficial when taking nighttime shots. It should also allow for sharper images when taking shots in daytime lighting because the sensor doesn't need to be open for as long. There's simply less chance for the image to be blurry.

Finally, photographers like to adjust the aperture because it gives them more creative control. Choosing a narrow aperture and extending the shutter time can capture stunning motion blur, for example.

In theory, bringing a custom aperture to the iPhone 18 Pro Max opens the door to all of these benefits. In reality, whether or not you see them will depend on how you use your iPhone's camera.

If you're an iPhone photographer and you like to dive in and tweak settings, you'll love the custom aperture. Apple has added new Pro Controls to the Camera app so you can tweak them to your heart's content.

But for the rest of us who just want to take a good photo with our phones, the custom aperture is less noticeable. We simply won't spend our time changing these settings to create the amazing images we know these phones can capture.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Pin-sharp images are the norm

The good news is the iPhone 18 Pro Max still has the ability to make automatic choices for all of the settings photographers like to tweak. And it does an excellent job of doing it, too.

I've been using the iPhone 18 Pro Max as a point-and-shoot camera, doing little more than tapping what I want to focus on. The results have been hugely impressive. Photos look great, videos are vibrant, and my iCloud storage is almost full. All signs of a good camera.

None of this is to say I haven't noticed any improvement as a result of that variable aperture. There's one big one, and it's very welcome.

I've never really been a fan of the iPhone's Night mode, the feature that captures as much light as possible in low-light situations. I've always found it to result in images that are too soft and overly bright.

But the iPhone 18 Pro Max's variable aperture has allowed me to turn Night mode off completely. And I'm able to take photos that much better resemble what I can see with my own two eyes. I'm a big fan.

48-megapixel Fusion Ultra Wide camera

The ultra wide camera is something that I rarely missed during my last year with the iPhone Air, but it's back with the iPhone 18 Pro Max. With its 48-megapixel sensor, it's capable of capturing some lovely images and videos at 0.5x.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: The ultra wide helps when you can't step any further away

The usefulness of a 0.5x camera will depend on your location and the subject you're trying to capture. I've said in previous reviews that I rarely find myself in need of such a camera, and that's still the case today.

But like many features, the iPhone's ultra wide camera is nice to have, just for those times when it proves to be useful. It helps that it does an admirable job when those times come around, including the iPhone's macro mode.

Apple's ultra wide cameras doing double duty as macro cameras is nothing new, of course. It's been doing it for years, and it's another nice-to-have feature. Just in case.

Designed for capturing close-ups of a subject, like a flower, the macro camera is more than up to the job. The Camera app automatically switches to macro mode when it's needed, but you can manually enable it as well.

48-megapixel Fusion Telephoto camera

Behind the main camera, the telephoto is the one I've found myself using the most during my testing. Like the other cameras, it has a large 48-megapixel sensor, but this time with a 4x optical zoom attached to it.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: A telephoto lens certainly has its uses

Apple's Camera app also offers an 8x zoom for those times when you need to get a little closer. But it's a faux zoom: Apple simply switches from capturing a 24-megapixel shot to a 12-megapixel one, punching in on the pixels in the center of the sensor.

For objects even further away, a 40x digital zoom is available. Let's just say that I suggest putting your iPhone back in your pocket and getting physically closer to your subject instead. Your photos will thank you for it.

That is to say, especially at 4x, the iPhone 18 Pro Max's telephoto camera takes excellent shots. And you might be surprised how often it comes in useful, from capturing a dog on a walk to getting a closer look at a new building in the distance.

Apple's decision to ditch the 12-megapixel telephoto camera for a 48-megapixel Fusion camera on the iPhone 17 Pro Max was a good one. It's a decision that remains so with its successor today.

While new cameras often drive new iPhone sales, Apple's new chips help bring new features to those cameras. They also make iPhones some of the best-performing phones in the world. One even powers the MacBook Neo.

For the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Apple introduced the A20 Pro. Built on TSMC's new 2nm platform, it's incredibly capable and impressively power-efficient.

Each A20 Pro ships with six CPU cores (two performance, four efficiency) and seven GPU cores with per-core Neural Accelerators. It also doubles the number of Neural Engine cores from 16 to 32 for the first time.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: The A20 Pro is a quick chip indeed

It's no surprise that Apple has brought even more Neural Engine cores to the iPhone, especially if it intends for the A20 Pro to be used in a future MacBook Neo.

These cores, coupled with improved GPU performance, make the A20 Pro the perfect chip for faster, local AI workloads. With Siri AI on board, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is best placed for faster responses and generative AI processing.

iPhone 18 Pro Max review: The A20 Pro excels in multi-core tests

Keeping that chip cool is a priority for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which is why Apple has expanded and redesigned its vapor chamber thermal design. It provides up to 40% better sustained performance for longer gaming sessions and video work. All while keeping the iPhone from getting too hot to the touch.

All of these changes, coupled with up to 50% increased memory bandwidth, make the iPhone 18 Pro Max a dream to use. It's fast, it's reliable, and it doesn't hiccup.

Of course, all of those things could be said about the A19 Pro, too. I never once found the iPhone Air lacking in performance. I highly doubt many iPhone 18 Pro Max buyers will, either.

My testing has shown the iPhone 18 Pro Max to be a capable gaming device, especially when paired with a controller. Touchscreens are great for some things, but I have yet to be convinced that gaming is one of them.

Games perform admirably, and, importantly, the iPhone 18 Pro Max has yet to get overly warm. It cools down pretty rapidly once the gaming gives way to my usual social scrolling and Reddit browsing.

Wrapping up the speeds and feeds section of this review, this iPhone uses Apple's N1 wireless networking chip. That means Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 7 support, with Thread networking tech thrown in.

Interestingly, the UK iPhone 18 Pro Max I've been testing uses Apple's C2 cellular modem. If you buy an iPhone 18 Pro in the United States, you'll get the same modem as well. But not if you choose the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

As for why that's the case, Apple hasn't said. What we do know is that the iPhone 18 Pro Max sold in the United States seems to be the only model not to use the C2. Whether that's down to Apple's ongoing agreement with Qualcomm, we may never know.

The good news is that it likely matters not one bit. Just a quirk of Apple's supply chain and no more.

Ever since the iPhone Pro and Pro Max received feature parity in terms of camera technologies, there are two reasons to choose the latter. The Pro Max has the larger display, which is important to some people. For others, it's all about the battery life.

Bigger displays mean bigger phones, and Apple can use that extra space to install larger batteries. The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a big ol' battery, and that's reflected in how it performs.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max is rated for up to 45 hours of video playback on a single charge. That sounds impressive but ultimately means very little.

That's why Apple now offers "typical use" figures, with a claimed iPhone 18 Pro Max battery life of up to 30 hours. The iPhone 18 Pro is rated for 24 hours.

I'm writing this review after a week with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I've found no reason to doubt Apple's claims. The first few days of any new iPhone are always full of app-installing and data-caching, so battery life often suffers.

But since then, I've found the iPhone 18 Pro Max to be every bit the battery life champ it's claimed to be. I can easily see it lasting two days between charges if needed, especially during light usage.

The good news keeps coming, too, because charging the iPhone 18 Pro Max is incredibly fast. Even a relatively short time connected to a charger can make a huge difference.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max can be charged to 50% capacity in around 15 minutes when using a charger rated for at least 60W. It'll need to be a charger that supports Adjustable Voltage Supply, so your older charger might not be up to the task.

Wireless charging is also surprisingly impressive. 30 minutes connected to a MagSafe charger will get you to 50% battery.

All of this is to say that even when an iPhone 18 Pro Max battery is low, getting it back to 50% or more isn't the chore it once was. Just remember Apple won't give you any kind of charger in the box, although it still ships iPhones with USB-C cables. For now, at least.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the best non-folding iPhone money can buy. For a lot of people, it will simply be the best iPhone, too. The iPhone Duo won't be for everyone, even if we put its $1,999 price to one side.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max also runs iOS 27, Apple's latest iPhone software. That brings new Apple Intelligence features and Siri AI, albeit in beta form for the time being.

It also means new child safety features. Accessibility improvements. A custom EQ for AirPods owners. Improved iCloud Shared Album support.

"Are you getting it?"

If you're someone who normally buys the biggest, best, and most feature-laden iPhone, you already know you're buying an iPhone 18 Pro Max. I'm here to tell you that you won't be disappointed with what you get.

But there's a wildcard. The iPhone Duo is the new king, but it's no Pro Max. It won't have a variable aperture, nor will it have a telephoto camera at all. There's no Face ID.

Money no object, the iPhone 18 Pro Max buying decision comes down to a trade-off. You need to decide which matters most to you. Better cameras and Face ID, or an iPhone that turns into an iPad.

I write this review still not knowing my answer to that question. Hopefully, by the time you read it, you'll know yours.

Rating 4.0 out of 5

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is for those who want the best features, the longest battery life, and the biggest display. Its new main camera will make these new Pro phones the go-to for photographers and videographers everywhere.

But if you buy the iPhone Pro Max because it's the coolest phone that Apple has to offer, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might not hit the spot. If you're ready for something new after years of big slabs of metal and glass, the iPhone Duo might be worth considering instead.
